strengths: Addresses a genuine and under-served gap: standardized, apples-to-apples evaluation of training-free representation-steering methods, with an explicit and novel emphasis on behavioral entanglement rather than a single target behavior.

The modular framework (direction generation, direction selection, direction application, intervention locations, conditional steering) is a clean, well-conceived abstraction that maps onto DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, and LAT and naturally extends to other combinations, which is a useful contribution beyond a single leaderboard.

Broad and thoughtfully organized behavioral coverage (17 datasets; three safety-relevant primary behaviors plus ten secondary behaviors across social, reasoning, epistemic-integrity, and normative categories), with primary/secondary separation enabling controlled study of out-of-distribution side effects.

The empirical finding that steering effectiveness and entanglement are jointly determined by the model/method/behavior combination (no universal best method), and that entanglement shows up in social behaviors (sycophancy, anthropomorphism) more than in the TruthfulQA/reasoning targets prior work emphasized, is a useful and actionable observation.

The Limitations section is unusually honest and specific (English-only, instruction-tuned models, static vectors, aggregate metrics, uniform grid search, 64-token generation, final-token extraction), which appropriately scopes the claims.
weaknesses: Empirical scope is thin relative to the claims: only two 7-8B instruction-tuned models and only five static, training-free vector methods. Claims that models are a 'key determinant' of steering performance and that differences reflect 'representational geometry' are not well supported by n=2 models.

The two aggregate metrics are questionable. Effectiveness normalizes by (1 - y_b), which strongly amplifies behaviors with high baseline performance and can let a single behavior dominate the aggregate; entanglement uses (1/|B_ood|) * sqrt(sum of squares), which is a non-standard formulation that scales with the number of OOD behaviors and makes the headline Pareto plots in Figure 2 sensitive to dataset composition.

The justification for using 20% subsets of each primary dataset ('reduces the likelihood of overfitting to static evaluation sets') is unconvincing; subsampling reduces statistical power and evaluation reliability rather than mitigating overfitting, and no variance/CI analysis is provided for any reported number.

All generation is capped at 64 tokens, which plausibly under-detects harmful content and hallucination that would surface later, directly affecting the primary results (refusal/SALAD ASR and hallucination rates) that anchor the paper's conclusions.

The analysis is largely descriptive (Figures 3-8 with absolute-percent-change heatmaps); mechanistic hypotheses (e.g., 'shared mechanisms in prompt interpretation') are asserted without any probing or evidence, leaving the central entanglement question under-explained.

Uniform grid-search direction selection across all methods may disadvantage methods that rely on behavior-specific selection, and this confound is acknowledged but not quantified; similarly, deviations from original implementations (e.g., standardizing selection) make it unclear whether reported differences reflect methods or the harness.

Reproducibility is unclear: the code link is incomplete ('https://github.com/'), and no per-method hyperparameter settings, seeds, or variance are reported; several datasets are generated with LLM judges (GPT-4o, Llama-3.3-70B) whose reliability is not validated.

No direct quantitative head-to-head with the closest existing benchmark (AxBench) despite positioning the work against it, so the added value of SteeringControl over prior standardized suites is argued rather than demonstrated.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: systematic evaluation of representation steering methods and their unintended side effects (entanglement).
Provides a modular framework that decomposes steering into direction generation, selection, and application, which could facilitate controlled comparisons and future method development.
Collects a diverse set of 17 datasets covering three primary safety-relevant behaviors (bias, harmful generation, hallucination) and ten secondary behaviors (e.g., sycophancy, morality, reasoning).
Evaluates five popular steering methods across two models, revealing tradeoffs between effectiveness and entanglement.
Includes an honest limitations section that acknowledges several constraints (e.g., English-only, static vectors, fixed token length).
weaknesses: Critical reproducibility flaw: all primary evaluations are conducted on a random 20% subset of each dataset, but the subset is not specified or released, making results non-comparable to future work and sensitive to random seed. This undermines the benchmark's core purpose.

No validation that the reimplemented steering methods match the original methods' behavior or reported results. The paper makes ad-hoc decisions when details are unclear (e.g., direction selection via grid search), but without verification, the benchmark may measure artifacts of the reimplementation rather than the methods themselves.

Lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests are reported, despite many comparisons across methods, models, and behaviors. The claimed findings (e.g., tradeoffs, model-specific differences) could be noise.

The aggregate metrics are ad hoc and not well justified. Effectiveness normalizes by (1 - y_b), which can be unstable when baseline performance is near 1; entanglement uses an unnormalized root-mean-square across heterogeneous scales, allowing high-variance behaviors to dominate.

Heavy reliance on LLM judges (GPT-4o, LlamaGuard-4, LLaMA-3.3-70B) for safety-critical evaluations (harmful generation, bias, sycophancy) without any validation of their reliability or agreement with human judgments.
Only two models (Qwen-2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B) are evaluated, which is insufficient to support broad conclusions about steering methods or to serve as a comprehensive benchmark.

Presentation issues: figures are low-resolution and difficult to read; the main results are shown only as heatmaps with no accompanying numerical tables; there are typos and citation errors (e.g., 'Grattafori et al., 2024', 'rditi et al.', 'Ant, 2024'); the code link is incomplete ('https://github.com/').
No ethics or broader impact statement is provided, despite the paper's focus on red-teaming harmful generation and bias, which raises dual-use concerns.

The benchmark's novelty relative to existing frameworks (e.g., AxBench, EasyEdit2) is not convincingly demonstrated; the paper does not show that existing benchmarks miss the specific entanglement phenomena it studies.

The findings are largely qualitative and expected (e.g., tradeoffs exist, model-specific differences, CAST reduces entanglement), without offering deep new insights or actionable guidance for method design.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: standardized evaluation of representation steering and behavioral entanglement, which is currently fragmented across datasets, methods, and definitions.

Provides a broad benchmark of 17 datasets spanning three primary safety-relevant behaviors (harmful generation/refusal, bias, hallucination) and ten secondary behaviors across social behavior, reasoning, epistemic integrity, and normative judgment.

Introduces a useful modular framework that decomposes training-free steering into direction generation, selection, and application, with interchangeable components that can support methods beyond the five evaluated.

Systematically compares five popular steering methods (DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, LAT) on two open models, including variants with/without KL checks and conditional steering, and reports per-behavior effects via heatmaps.

Delivers concrete empirical findings: no single method dominates across models/behaviors, entanglement can extend to social behaviors such as sycophancy and anthropomorphism, and CAST often improves the effectiveness-entanglement tradeoff.

Dataset construction is described with fixed train/validation/test splits, stratification, and negative examples to support contrastive direction generation, which aids reproducibility if data/code are released.

The limitations section is unusually thorough and honest, acknowledging English/instruction-tuned scope, static vector interventions, uniform grid search, short generation length, and exclusion of reasoning models.
The work lays useful groundwork for future steering methods that explicitly optimize the effectiveness-entanglement Pareto frontier.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is limited to two 7B/8B instruction-tuned models and five steering methods, so broad claims about method rankings and entanglement may not generalize to larger, multilingual, or reasoning models.

Primary evaluations are conducted on 20% subsets of the benchmark without multiple seeds or confidence intervals, and several secondary datasets contain only ~110 prompts; this makes reported differences and entanglement scores vulnerable to high variance.
There is no uncertainty quantification, statistical testing, or seed variation, so the central comparisons and Pareto curves may not be statistically reliable.

The effectiveness and entanglement metrics are ad hoc and not well justified; the entanglement formula (1/|B| times the square root of summed squared differences) has non-standard scaling, is not normalized by baseline performance, and can make values hard to interpret across behavior sets.

Method comparisons may be confounded by the standardized grid-search selection procedure and other implementation choices, potentially disadvantaging methods relative to their original hyperparameter tuning; the authors acknowledge this risk.

Many behaviors are scored by LLM judges (GPT-4o, LlamaGuard-4, LLaMA-3.3-70B) without human validation or inter-judge agreement, and some negative examples are generated by GPT-4.1-mini or randomly selected, raising concerns about benchmark validity.
Reproducibility is weakened by an incomplete code URL, unclear dataset release details, and insufficient specification of judge prompts, sampling seeds, and exact data versions.

The presentation is dense: main figures are difficult-to-read heatmaps, Figure 2 and the metric aggregation are ambiguous (e.g., what is averaged across objectives/behaviors), and the selective exclusion of TwinViews for Llama affects comparability of entanglement scores.
Dual-use and ethical considerations around steering to increase harmful generation/jailbreaking are not discussed beyond standard limitations, despite the safety-sensitive nature of the benchmark.

Originality is moderate: related benchmarks such as AxBench, EasyEdit2, and Im & Li (2025) already standardize steering evaluation, so the main novelty lies in the entanglement focus and safety-behavior coverage rather than a fundamentally new method.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: systematic evaluation of cross-safety-perspective entanglement in representation steering, which prior frameworks (AxBench, EasyEdit2) do not cover. The multi-perspective framing (refusal, hallucination, bias, social behaviors, reasoning, epistemic integrity, normative judgment) is a useful organizing contribution.

Technically solid and reproducible: the modular decomposition into direction generation/selection/application is clearly specified, hyperparameter grids, KL filter, splits, prompts, and per-experiment hyperparameters (Tables 5–13) are documented, and computational cost is estimated. Human-LLM judge agreement is reported for key judges.

Comprehensive empirical sweep: 5 methods × 5 steering targets × 3 main models (plus 2 smaller Qwen scales), 3 settings (Standard/NoKL/Conditional), with FDR-corrected significance markers in the appendix.

Several genuinely interesting findings that go beyond a naive expectation: jailbreaking does not uniformly increase toxicity, hallucination steering shifts political views in opposite directions across models, and improving one bias sub-type can degrade the other. The signed entanglement decomposition (Table 16) and the conditional-steering Pareto analysis (Figure 4) add nuance.

Honest and careful framing: the paper explicitly separates empirical findings from the superposition hypothesis, avoids mechanistic/causal claims, and includes a candid limitations section and impact statement addressing the jailbreaking dual-use concern.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely descriptive measurement. The paper explicitly states it does not make causal claims and offers only non-identifiable hypotheses for method-level differences, so the central scientific insight reduces to 'interventions have model/method/perspective-dependent side effects'—useful but shallow for a top-tier venue without deeper analysis.

Originality is mainly in evaluation scope: the five steering methods are reimplementations of existing work (DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, LAT) and CAST-style conditional gating is adopted from prior work. No new method or theoretical result is introduced.

Asymmetric normalization undermines several comparisons: Effectiveness is normalized by remaining headroom (1−y_d) while Entanglement is left unnormalized. This makes cross-perspective statements such as 'refusal suppression is substantially more effective than hallucination or bias reduction' potentially artifacts of differing baselines/headroom rather than intrinsic steerability, and it weakens the effectiveness/entanglement ratios in Table 2.

Key headline numbers are hard to trace from the main text. Claims such as 'degradation up to 76%' on social behaviors, 'up to 26%' on commonsense morality, and the ±25–28% political shifts are not tied to specific (method, model, setting) cells in the main text, and the main-text figures (e.g., Figure 3/4) are aggregates that do not obviously surface these extremes.

Many (method, perspective) cells show near-zero or negative effectiveness (e.g., CAA and PCA on several perspectives in Figure 2 and Table 2). For these cells, entanglement is measured on interventions that failed to move the target behavior, so the 'entanglement' numbers carry limited interpretive weight yet are aggregated into the central narrative.

Evaluation relies heavily on LLM judges, with acknowledged only-moderate agreement for DarkBench (κ≈0.71), and generation is capped at 64 tokens without reasoning. The authors concede conclusions on DarkBench behaviors 'should be read as indicative trends,' which constrains the strength of the social-behavior and epistemic-integrity findings.

strengths: Addresses a timely and relevant problem: quantifying cross-behavior interference ("entanglement") of representation-steering interventions, an area where the community lacks systematic safety-focused evaluation.

Broad empirical sweep: nine safety perspectives, 18 datasets, five steering methods, and five models (Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B plus two smaller Qwen models) with per-dataset, per-method breakdowns and FDR-corrected significance markers.

The modular decomposition of steering into direction generation/selection/application is a genuinely reusable engineering contribution that enables apples-to-apples method comparison and novel combinations (e.g., CAST-style conditional steering).

Honest limitations and ethics discussion (jailbreaking risk scoped, judge-bias caveat, reproducibility caveats about unspecified operational details), plus reported human–LLM judge agreement (κ = 0.86/0.92 for PreciseWiki/SALAD-Bench).

Some actionable and non-obvious observations, e.g., conditional (CAST) steering yielding Pareto improvements on refusal/hallucination but not bias, and PCA vs CAA entangling with different OOD behaviors when steering extrinsic hallucination.
Good reproducibility scaffolding: detailed hyperparameter tables (layers/coefficients/thresholds), prompt templates, and compute estimates.
weaknesses: The central metric is not comparable across perspectives, yet the headline claims depend on such comparison. Entanglement is RMS absolute drift and is deliberately left unnormalized; because perspectives differ in baseline, remaining headroom, and dataset count, statements like "social behaviors and normative judgment consistently incur the highest entanglement" and "degradation up to 76%" are confounded. The authors' argument against normalization (a 1% drift on a 99% baseline inflating to match a 100% drift on a 0% baseline) is a strawman — sensible normalization (e.g., by headroom or baseline variance) is possible.

The Effectiveness/Entanglement ratio (Table 2) divides a headroom-normalized effectiveness by an unnormalized absolute entanglement, mixing incommensurable units, which makes the ratio hard to interpret and undermines the practitioner guidance derived from it.

The findings are largely confirmatory: that steering one behavior perturbs others and that effects are (method, model, perspective)-dependent is unsurprising, and the paper itself concedes the method-level accounts are "non-identifiable" and mutually compatible with a trivial reading ("each method captures different amounts of extraneous variance").

Limited novelty relative to existing work: AxBench, EasyEdit2, and prior steering side-effect studies are cited as close; the multi-perspective safety framing is an incremental extension rather than a new method or new understanding.

Asymmetry in scope: refusal is only steered in the jailbreak (suppression) direction; the safety-increasing direction is omitted (with some justification), so conclusions about refusal entanglement are one-sided and may not generalize to the full steering space.

Some headline numbers are not clearly sourced or appear unit-inconsistent (e.g., the "up to 76%" degradation, "25% right to 28% left" political shifts, and the +213.5/+213.7 values in the Gemma NoKL table), which raises questions about metric reliability and coding.

Potential selection/leakage concerns: the KL-divergence filter and validation selection use Alpaca with the same split as the refusal perspective, and only a single KL threshold (0.1) is explored; the choice of validation objective for grid search may bias toward the steered target.

Presentation and reference errors: garbled/mangled citations (e.g., "Bais and Saha (2021)" for Bai et al., "Maizeika et al." for Mazeika/Weidinger), and an out-of-place main-text reference to the appendix-only Qwen-2.5-1.5B experiment.

The "Why Entanglement May Arise" section is explicitly speculative and adds little beyond a superposition hypothesis that the authors admit is unvalidated at scale; it reads as filler rather than contribution.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-executed benchmark: nine safety perspectives across 18 datasets, five steering methods (DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, LAT), and multiple models (Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B plus smaller Qwen scales), totaling ~280 experiments. This is a substantial and genuinely useful evaluation infrastructure.

The modular decomposition of steering into direction generation, selection, and application is a clean and reusable design that enables method-agnostic comparison and novel combinations (e.g., conditional/CAST steering), which is a real contribution beyond a simple leaderboard.

Careful methodological hygiene: KL-divergence filtering on Alpaca, headroom-normalized effectiveness, stratified splits, FDR-corrected significance tests, and a signed Harm/Benef decomposition of the entanglement metric. The decision to report absolute (unnormalized) entanglement is explicitly justified.
Honest and thorough limitations discussion (Appendix A) and an appropriate impact statement addressing the dual-use nature of the refusal-suppression direction.

Reproducibility-relevant details are documented: hyperparameter grids, selected layers/coefficients (Tables 5-15), LLM-judge prompts, human-LLM agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.86-0.92 for PreciseWiki/SALAD-Bench), and compute estimates.

The empirical findings are practically relevant (e.g., social behaviors most vulnerable, conditional steering as a Pareto improvement on some perspectives), and the paper correctly refrains from making mechanistic causal claims, offering superposition only as a labeled hypothesis.
weaknesses: The paper is fundamentally descriptive. It reports which (method, model, perspective) combinations entangle but offers no causal/mechanistic account, and the authors themselves concede multiple non-identifiable accounts are compatible with the data. The 'Key Findings' are thus closer to a well-organized survey than to a mechanistic result.

The framing overstates the magnitude of the phenomenon. Entanglement is typically small in absolute terms (mostly <10%, with reasoning <2%), yet the abstract/conclusion call it 'a first-order concern' and cite 'degradation up to 76%' by cherry-picking worst cases. The headline '28% left / 25% right' political shifts are model-dependent outliers, not central tendencies, and would benefit from clearer calibration of practical significance.

Some claimed 'counterintuitive' results are not clearly counterintuitive or novel: that jailbreaking does not uniformly increase toxicity is consistent with prior refusal-direction work (Arditi et al., 2024), and the bias-steering effects are so small (<20% effectiveness, many negative effectiveness/entanglement ratios) that conclusions drawn from them are weakly supported.

Comparison to closely related frameworks (AxBench, EasyEdit2) is relegated to two sentences in Related Work; there is no head-to-head empirical positioning or discussion of what SteeringSafety adds beyond dataset breadth, which weakens the originality argument.

Generalization is limited: cross-scale claims rest on a single model family (Qwen-2.5), and the main models are relatively small; the paper does not test whether the entanglement patterns hold at frontier scale, which matters for the deployment-oriented motivation.

Reproducibility is not fully guaranteed: there is no explicit statement that the benchmark/code and curated splits are publicly released, and several results tables/figures in the manuscript are garbled or appear as unreadable images, making some reported numbers hard to verify.

The entanglement metric's design choices (unnormalized absolute drift, TwinViews excluded from signed decomposition, likelihood vs. substring scoring switching across datasets) introduce comparability caveats that the main-text aggregate figures partly obscure, and the effectiveness/entanglement ratio mixes quantities of different units.

Only five steering targets are actually steered (refusal, intrinsic/extrinsic hallucination, explicit/implicit bias); the remaining 'perspectives' are only ever evaluated as OOD targets, so the benchmark does not actually measure entanglement for most perspectives as the framing might suggest.
